claims.text: Q235 steel's native surface oxide is composed mainly of Fe3O4 and Fe2O3.
The native oxide on Q235 steel acts as an effective passivation layer under ambient conditions.
At 700–900 °C in aggressive chloride salts, the native oxide loses integrity through phase transformation and dissolution.
Loss of native-oxide integrity leads to accelerated corrosion of Q235 steel.
As-received Q235 steel has an intact, naturally formed oxide film before exposure.
At room temperature, the native oxides remain compact and protective in a chloride-containing environment.
High-temperature exposure transforms the oxide into a porous or non-adherent scale.
Reaction with chloride salts can form volatile or soluble iron chloride compounds.
The stability, phase composition, and microstructural integrity of the native iron-oxide film mediate Q235 corrosion behavior.
At room temperature, the native oxide limits ionic transport through the surface.
At 700–900 °C, oxide transformation or dissolution breaks down passivation and exposes the underlying steel to enhanced oxidation and pitting.
Q235 samples exposed at 700–900 °C will exhibit greater mass change than samples exposed at room temperature.
High-temperature samples will develop porous transformed oxide scales and localized pitting.
XRD analysis of high-temperature samples will reveal phase transitions in the oxide layer.
Room-temperature chloride exposure of Q235 with an intact native oxide should produce relatively low corrosion rates and minimal mass change.
Surface treatments that alter the native oxide may change the proposed corrosion behavior.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to salts that do not promote oxide dissolution or transformation, such as non-chloride salts.
Removing the native oxide should substantially alter corrosion behavior if native-oxide transformation governs degradation.
